# [$1-a-year OpenAI is over. Federal agencies now get 50% off](https://substack.com/redirect/2bddf7ad-b8a0-4aa4-a81e-7e062a2af7a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The General Services Administration locked a OneGov pact giving federal, state, local and tribal agencies a 50% discount on OpenAI's most advanced models with no minimum spend.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2bddf7ad-b8a0-4aa4-a81e-7e062a2af7a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **FedRAMP-only access:** The agreement applies GSA AI terms and confines model use to environments already authorized under the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program.
* **Try-before-you-buy:** Acting Federal Acquisition Service Commissioner Laura Stanton said OneGov AI deals exist so agencies can test tools on a consumption basis before a lengthy acquisition.
* **Altman backs the pact:** OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said secure access can make government more efficient, strengthen cybersecurity and improve services people rely on.
* **Door left open:** Stanton invited other AI vendors to bring capabilities through OneGov, saying GSA wants more choice, competition and taxpayer value.

* **Third-quarter beat landed:** Profit was $1.83 billion, or $4.62 a share, versus $1.77 billion, or $4.18, a year earlier. Adjusted earnings were $6.13 versus FactSet's $6.08 forecast.
* **Subscriptions carried revenue:** Sales rose 13% to $6.76 billion against a $6.69 billion FactSet estimate, with subscription revenue climbing to $6.58 billion from $5.79 billion.

# [Record 6.1% private-credit defaults meet a $100 oil shock](https://substack.com/redirect/2bddf7ad-b8a0-4aa4-a81e-7e062a2af7a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Fitch's U.S. private-credit default rate hit a record 6.1% in the 12 months through July as oil near $100 and a possible Fed hike squeeze floating-rate borrowers.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2bddf7ad-b8a0-4aa4-a81e-7e062a2af7a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* **Double hit on EBITDA:** Benefit Street's Anant Kumar said energy-driven inflation, not rates alone, is the risk: 3.4% CPI plus an energy shock squeezes earnings while floating coupons rise.
* **SOFR resets fast:** Direct-lending loans typically price over SOFR. Kumar said a 25-basis-point hike feeds quickly into portfolios, lifting lender yield first, then losses if weak credits miss payments.
* **Rolling refinance wall:** Raymond James' Sunaina Sinha Haldea said the wall will arrive as amendments, extensions, equity injections and restructurings, not one event, with coverage already near 1x at stressed names.
* **How far yields must go:** Nomura's Matthew Pallai said another 50 to 100-plus basis points would be needed to force widespread default concern. Thursday's 10-year yield jumped more than 11 basis points to 4.954%.

Reflecting on the courage, sacrifice, and strength that carried America through our darkest hour| | |
---
Twenty-five years ago today, our nation changed forever. On September 11, 2001, an act of unimaginable evil sought to break the spirit of the United States. **Thousands of innocent souls – mothers, fathers, sons, daughters, and friends – were taken from us far too soon at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and in a quiet field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.** Yet, in our darkest hour, the world witnessed the unmatched courage and resolve that defines the American spirit. We saw first responders – firefighters, police officers, and paramedics – unhesitatingly run directly toward danger, risking and giving their lives to save strangers. We saw everyday citizens demonstrate incredible heroism, holding the line in the skies above Pennsylvania to protect countless others. **For data integrity purposes, please do not complete this survey if your email address is not dpwillis67@gmail.com.**
---
Folks, The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964, **prohibits both Congress and the states from conditioning the right to vote in federal elections on payment of a poll tax or any other type of tax**. Poll taxes for State and local elections were declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in the case _Harper vs. Virginia State Board of Elections_. However, supporters of voting rights allege that voter identification requirements passed in recent legislation amount to a modern-day poll tax. Texas, for example, requires photo ID to vote, yet each of those methods -- _a Texas Driver's License, Texas Personal Identification Card, or Texas Handgun License_ \-- cost money to acquire. In addition, their other acceptable forms of ID have a cost -- both a United States Passport and United States Citizenship Certificate must be purchased, and a United States Military Identification Card requires military service or work as a contractor._We're looking to see how our supporters feel about this issue. Please take our quick survey:_
---
| | |
# **Team: Do you believe states like Texas are violating laws regarding poll taxes by requiring paid forms of ID to vote?**
---

Folks, The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964, prohibits both Congress and the states from conditioning the right to vote in federal elections on payment of a poll tax or any other type of tax. Poll taxes for State and local elections were declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in the case Harper vs. Virginia State Board of Elections. However, supporters of voting rights allege that voter identification requirements passed in recent legislation amount to a modern-day poll tax. Texas, for example, requires photo ID to vote, yet each of those methods -- a Texas Driver's License, Texas Personal Identification Card, or Texas Handgun License \-- cost money to acquire. In addition, their other acceptable forms of ID have a cost -- both a United States Passport and United States Citizenship Certificate must be purchased, and a United States Military Identification Card requires military service or work as a contractor.We're looking to see how our supporters feel about this issue. body:

**Friend of Life,** When Isabella told the father of her baby she was pregnant, she was hoping for encouragement. Instead, she received a single text message. **"Abort."** Already grieving the loss of her toddler's father to cancer, Isabella suddenly found herself carrying another child without the support she desperately needed. Fear quickly gave way to hopelessness, and she became convinced there was only one way out of the situation she was facing. Then something unexpected happened. Instead of making a permanent decision she could never take back, Isabella found her way to a PreBorn! Network Clinic, where she was welcomed with compassion and surrounded by people who cared about both her and her baby. They listened to her story, answered her questions, talked honestly about parenting and adoption, and shared the hope of Jesus Christ with her. As those conversations continued, our staff introduced Isabella to Cari and Christian, a couple who had spent years praying that God would bless them with the opportunity to adopt a little girl. Months later, when Isabella gave birth, she spent 80 precious hours holding her daughter before placing her into Cari and Christian's arms. Then she quietly said the words they will never forget: **"You are going to be parents to Liliana."** What Isabella didn't know was that Cari and Christian had already chosen that very name years earlier while praying for the daughter they hoped God would one day provide. Only God could write a story like that. Every day at PreBorn!, we meet women who believe their circumstances will define the rest of their lives. Time and again, God reminds us that His plans are often greater than anything we could imagine. Your generosity helps make those moments possible. A gift of **$28 helps provide one life-saving ultrasound** , giving another woman the opportunity to slow down, receive compassionate care, and hear that both she and her baby are deeply loved by Jesus Christ. And because of a generous matching challenge, **every gift made before September 30 will be MATCHED dollar for dollar, up to $100,000.** Will you help another woman discover that hope is never beyond God's reach?
---

25 years ago, on September 11th, 2001, I was nine years old, which means I belong to the last generation that can say, "I remember America before 9/11."
I remember the morning itself, the distress, the confusion, the television on at six in the morning, young me calling over to my mother in the kitchen where she was making breakfast when the second plane hit the tower, the images that corporate media played over and over and over again, inescapably, on every channel.
Nearly three thousand human beings were killed that day in New York, at the Pentagon, and aboard Flight 93. They deserved grief, honor, and dignity. What they got afterward was a transformation of their country into something unrecognizable.
There are two ledgers here. There's the devastating impact of the day itself, and there is the vastly larger cost in blood, treasure, liberty, trust, international standing, and human possibility that Americans and millions of other people paid because of what our government chose to do in response. I remember that part beginning, too.

There was extraordinary national unity after the attacks, flags everywhere, neighbors looking after each other, people giving blood, a brief, almost physical sense that underneath everything that divided us, we belonged to each other. And then alongside it, fear, anger, suspicion.
As a fifth grader, I started hearing about Muslims, Sikhs, and other minorities being attacked. Turban-wearing Americans were assaulted by fellow Americans who knew so little about either Sikhism or Islam that grief and rage and ignorance had collapsed millions of individual human beings into a single imagined enemy.
After 9/11, my husband's mosque in Washington State was attacked many times, including while he was visiting as an American soldier on home leave, taking a few quiet minutes to meditate in peace. One time, interestingly, the rock that came through the window and hit him was thrown by young Latino men whose parents were undocumented, who told him directly when he conducted a citizen's arrest on them that they wanted to prove their patriotism to America by attacking a mosque. Never mind the Americans, including American soldiers, inside. Nationally, FBI statistics recorded a more than 1600% increase in anti-Islamic hate crime incidents in 2001.
Four days after the attacks, Sikh American Balbir Singh Sodhi was murdered at his Arizona gas station, the first reported killing in that backlash. His killer called himself a patriot. Now, I have Sikh American friends. I've spent meaningful time in gurdwaras. If you've not had the pleasure of meeting this community yourself, one of the first things I would want you to understand is the ethic built into their tradition. Feed people, any people. Serve people. Show up. Care for the community. Defend human dignity.
These Americans were and are our neighbors, and their fellow Americans attacked them. Even at nine years old, I understood something was terribly wrong with that - because America had taught me something different: equality, due process, religious freedom, liberty, and justice for all.

And then came Iraq. Before the invasion even began, my military family protested it. In February 2003, millions of people around the world took to the streets, and the demonstrations were relentless for years after. February 15th, 2003, has been described as among the largest coordinated protests in human history. Guinness records the roughly three-million-person rally in Rome as the largest anti-war demonstration on record. Every major American city had one.
I remember standing at our local protest in San Diego with my mother and my younger sister. My mother was carrying this enormous sign that said, "Navy Wife for Peace." Television cameras interviewed her with her two little girls alongside. You can sum up much of my life in the contradiction on that sign, because my father was a Navy doctor, and while his wife and daughters were marching against this war, he was already deployed into it. That contradiction became the architecture of my childhood.
Our family was raised inside my father's military career. He served honorably and with genuine humanity. And the war, which never should have been executed, was tearing us apart. One deployment, then another, then an extension. I started acting out at school. My grades fell. I remember the crushing sense of responsibility that can settle onto a child who understands far too much and can control absolutely nothing.
When he was gone, I would go into my parents' bedroom and put my head on his pillow just to breathe the comfort of his scent. He had one visit home. I remember lying on his chest and crying myself to sleep. I kept a photograph of my parents together in my desk at school. I would sneak looks at it during class. It reminded me of before, before the war, before everything felt like this.
Here's something we now know that a nine-year-old watching American television would never have known at the time. Iraq had nothing to do with those attacks. The hijackers, as far as the corporate media told us, were Al-Qaeda, and they were mostly Saudi. Even the strangely composed 9/11 Commission found no evidence that Iraq and Al-Qaeda had developed a collaborative operational relationship and **no evidence** that Iraq cooperated in planning or carrying out attacks against the United States.
The weapons of mass destruction used as a central justification for the invasion were not found. Even America's think tank, the Iraq Survey Group, concluded that Saddam Hussein's nuclear program had ended in 1991 and found no evidence of a serious effort to restart it.
That is not what Americans were told in 2002 and 2003. Benjamin Netanyahu came before Congress in September 2002 and told American lawmakers there was "no question whatsoever" Saddam Hussein was pursuing nuclear weapons. He warned that without severe American military action, the terror network would soon have nuclear weapons, too. That lands... _differently_ now.

Against the emphatic protest of millions of people in the streets all over the world, including us here at home, America invaded Iraq. I was 11 years old. During those years, I learned a phrase I came to hate, "collateral damage."
It's such a bloodless phrase, so self-righteous. It covers so much unnecessary pain. It can mean somebody's child, somebody's mother, somebody's leg, somebody's farm, their home, their school, somebody's entire previous universe of understanding what tomorrow was going to look like.
My father was a doctor, and for better or worse, he did not entirely believe in sheltering his eldest daughter from reality. He showed me photographs. His patients were American soldiers and Iraqi civilians, human beings who had encountered shrapnel, explosions, bullets, and kinetic force. After enough violence has been done to a human body, nationality becomes remarkably difficult to determine.
That shaped me. Politics was never exactly theoretical after that. War certainly wasn't. Bloody wounds and bereaved loved ones don't argue about how you voted.
Folks, it's been 25 years. Let's take stock. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the post-9/11 wars have cost the United States roughly $8 trillion in appropriations and obligations alone, including the long-term cost of caring for wounded veterans.
Eight. Trillion. Dollars.
That is public wealth, at generational scale, that could have built homes, schools, hospitals, transit, childcare, clean energy, roads, bridges. Could have funded universal healthcare, free college and childcare, reparations, high-speed rail. "Opportunity costs" can sound abstract, so let me be specific. **It is the country we did not become.**
The human ledger is worse. Researchers estimate that more than five million people died in America's major post-9/11 war zones through 2023, both directly from violence, and indirectly from destroyed health systems, malnutrition, disease, wrecked infrastructure, and economic collapse. At least 40 million people were made homeless.

At some point, numbers that large almost defeat comprehension. So I come back to one little girl hiding a photograph of her parents in her school desk. Because somewhere in Iraq, there was another child with a similar photograph, and somewhere in Afghanistan, and somewhere in Pakistan, Yemen, Syria, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Iran. In these and many more somewheres, there were mothers trying to explain to a child something that should never have happened and that they did nothing to cause.
Let's not forget the war did not remain overseas. The 9/11 attacks were used as a lever to transform American government and society. Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act on October 26th, 2001. The name really is an acronym, _**U** niting and **S** trengthening **A** merica by **P** roviding **A** ppropriate **T** ools **R** equired to **I** ntercept and **O** bstruct **T** errorism._
With its passage, the foundations of the modern surveillance state were laid. Americans would never have consented to this intrusive usurpation of our rights and freedoms in a time of peace. For certain agencies and corporations that serve paranoia, it's been an extraordinarily profitable change.
Also, the Department of Homeland Security was first created in 2002. Twenty-two agencies were assembled under it in a process taking years. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE itself, emerged from that restructuring in 2003. In earlier times, immigration was handled through Labor, not through Security.
And some of the changes stayed almost invisible. Shortly after 9/11, USCIS created the Controlled Application Review and Resolution Program, CARRP for short, which the ACLU calls, "Muslims Need Not Apply." Congress, which holds the sole power to make immigration law, declined to authorize this eleven times, but USCIS secretly implemented a special track for immigration applications flagged as national security concerns.
Thing is, the criteria they use are, 1, secret, 2, usually innocuous, and 3, unable to ever be challenged or addressed to clear their name. Civil liberties organizations have successfully challenged CARRP in court. It's secretive and discriminatory, particularly toward applicants from Muslim, Arab, Middle Eastern, and South Asian backgrounds. Most Americans have never heard of it. I didn't know about it until a few years ago. My husband, a decorated, disabled US military veteran, has been caught up in it for two decades.

These things became part of the institutional architecture of the country we all grew up in. They shaped our lives in countless ways, including the painful and **extremely direct through line between Abu Ghraib, which shattered what was left of my innocence, Guantanamo Bay, and modern-day ICE detention.**
Intelligence agents and soldiers who follow their lead, who are permitted or encouraged to commit war crimes, atrocities, murder, torture, and cruel and unusual punishment in America's name and who face no consequences, continue to climb in their careers, eventually get rotated back home, eventually retire out of the military and join the local police, prison guards, and ICE.
The attitude doesn't stay overseas. It comes home to our streets, to our neighborhoods, to our communities. The cruelty, the indifference, the mindset of supremacy, the casual willingness to abuse Black and brown people and justify it in the language of war and self-defense may prove one of the most lasting and consequential harvests of the post-9/11 era, and one that I suspect we'll regret deeply for a very long time to come.
And that's what I've spent 25 years trying to understand, because I remember before. I remember singing as a small child, "And I'm proud to be an American, where at least I know I'm free." Meant every word. There was something open-hearted about the patriotism I remember from early childhood. Then the patriotic music... changed. Same flags, same melodies, different emotional register. Something harder entered it, something more frightened, something much less tolerant of dissent.
Even the government's instruction to ordinary people felt strange. In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, President Bush told Americans to go shopping. I remember hearing that as a child and thinking, "Really? That's it? That's what citizenship and civic engagement requires of us? Mindless consumption?"
My family had taught me something different. My father loved to quote Thomas Paine, "I may not agree with what you have to say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it." My mother sang us a lullaby "Let there be peace on earth, and let it begin with me" Apparently, I took those to heart.

Over the years, as my trust in institutions deteriorated, I investigated everything, including the engineering. I've read the official account. I've also read the architects and engineers who have spent two decades arguing that the official account does not fully explain what they saw. They said that the towers came down in ways that resemble controlled demolition more than fire-induced failure. And they point out that Building 7, never struck by a plane, fell in its own footprint at nearly free-fall speed.
Now, NIST spent years on this. Its conclusion was fire-induced collapse. I am not an engineer. I'm not going to pretend to adjudicate it. But 25 years later, a substantial number of credentialed professionals still do not find the official explanation adequate. They have petitioned for a new investigation. They have not gotten one.
Here's the thing. **A nation confident in its own account of a defining catastrophe should not be afraid to answer the questions of its own engineers.**
Now, distrust is not evidence, but neither is authority. My mother, bless her heart, raised me to question authority and taught me that any legitimate authority would answer you gladly, promptly, and completely.
Early on, I believed my country would never lie to me about something this important. Not sure about that anymore. And the fact that I've lost that confidence, that millions of us no longer believe this, is itself one of the profound costs of the last 25 years.

I remember President Bush landing on the USS Abraham Lincoln in 2003 beneath that enormous Mission Accomplished banner, claiming that the battles were over and the war was won. In hindsight, I'm pretty sure that was a PR stunt to tell the protesters that we could go home now. The war, of course, had not ended.
I was 10, then 11, then 12, at once the child of a deployed military doctor, a victim of family separation, a witness to human suffering, and utterly powerless to change the foreign policy producing it. That complicated moral injury has shaped me in permanent ways. I'm sure I'm not the only one.
25 years later, the progressive destruction of my unquestioning trust in my country has been one of the most painful experiences of my life, and strangely, one of the most liberating.
Because patriotism no longer has to mean believing that America has always lived up to its ideals. It can mean deciding that those ideals belong to us, whether our institutions honor them or not. **Equality before the law, due process, freedom of conscience, human dignity, government accountable to the people it serves, liberty and justice for all.** Those words mattered to the nine-year-old girl I was. They matter more to me now.

And that is the accounting I want us to make on this anniversary. Not only who attacked us, truly, not just in media portrayals, but -
what did we become afterward?
What did we spend and why?
Who profited?
Whom did we hurt?
To whom did we grant impunity or power?
What did we surrender?
Did we trade essential liberty for temporary safety?
Where has that gotten us?
What did fear persuade us to tolerate that we never would have accepted before?
**And what parts of ourselves are we ready to recover?**
The people murdered on September 11th deserved genuine remembrance, grief unpolluted by the drums of war.
The American service members and their families sent into a quarter century of nonstop continuing wars deserved far more than blind nationalistic slogans.
The civilians whose countries became battlefields deserve to exist in our accounting at minimum, as they surely deserve to exist in their actual lives.
The Muslims and Sikhs and immigrants who discovered that their neighbors or their government suddenly regarded them with suspicion or worse belong in this history too.
So do the children waiting for deployed parents to come home, hoping they would, afraid they might not, unable to anticipate how difficult even those homecomings could be.
I was one of them, and I remember before.

25 years is long enough to mourn.
It is long enough to study, count, pay attention.
It's long enough to admit what we got wrong, and it's long enough to decide what lessons we intend to carry into the next 25.
For my part, the commitment I made as a child remains remarkably simple.
Peace is not the same as passivity.
**Patriotism is not the same as obedience.**
And love of country does not require pretending your country is incapable of wrongdoing.
It can require exactly the opposite, **taking its highest promises seriously enough to hold on to them even when power does not.**
I'm Melissa Chaudhry.
Care, Courage, the Constitution - and the promise I learned before I knew how difficult it would be to keep:

**liberty and justice for all.**

Will we allow those choices to shape the next 25 years? | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? | | Since I was 9 years old, America has taken the path of death, destruction, discrimination, and division, instead of purpose, unity, and peace. Will we allow those choices to shape the next 25 years? | | | Sep 11 | | | | | | | | | | | | 25 years ago, on September 11th, 2001, I was nine years old, which means I belong to the last generation that can say, "I remember America before 9/11." I remember the morning itself, the distress, the confusion, the television on at six in the morning, young me calling over to my mother in the kitchen where she was making breakfast when the second plane hit the tower, the images that corporate media played over and over and over again, inescapably, on every channel. Nearly three thousand human beings were killed that day in New York, at the Pentagon, and aboard Flight 93. They deserved grief, honor, and dignity. What they got afterward was a transformation of their country into something unrecognizable. There are two ledgers here. There's the devastating impact of the day itself, and there is the vastly larger cost in blood, treasure, liberty, trust, international standing, and human possibility that Americans and millions of other people paid because of what our government chose to do in response. I remember that part beginning, too. There was extraordinary national unity after the attacks, flags everywhere, neighbors looking after each other, people giving blood, a brief, almost physical sense that underneath everything that divided us, we belonged to each other. And then alongside it, fear, anger, suspicion. As a fifth grader, I started hearing about Muslims, Sikhs, and other minorities being attacked. Turban-wearing Americans were assaulted by fellow Americans who knew so little about either Sikhism or Islam that grief and rage and ignorance had collapsed millions of individual human beings into a single imagined enemy. After 9/11, my husband's mosque in Washington State was attacked many times, including while he was visiting as an American soldier on home leave, taking a few quiet minutes to meditate in peace. One time, interestingly, the rock that came through the window and hit him was thrown by young Latino men whose parents were undocumented, who told him directly when he conducted a citizen's arrest on them that they wanted to prove their patriotism to America by attacking a mosque. Never mind the Americans, including American soldiers, inside. Nationally, FBI statistics recorded a more than 1600% increase in anti-Islamic hate crime incidents in 2001. Four days after the attacks, Sikh American Balbir Singh Sodhi was murdered at his Arizona gas station, the first reported killing in that backlash. His killer called himself a patriot. Now, I have Sikh American friends. I've spent meaningful time in gurdwaras. If you've not had the pleasure of meeting this community yourself, one of the first things I would want you to understand is the ethic built into their tradition. Feed people, any people. Serve people. Show up. Care for the community. Defend human dignity. These Americans were and are our neighbors, and their fellow Americans attacked them. Even at nine years old, I understood something was terribly wrong with that - because America had taught me something different: equality, due process, religious freedom, liberty, and justice for all. And then came Iraq. Before the invasion even began, my military family protested it. In February 2003, millions of people around the world took to the streets, and the demonstrations were relentless for years after. February 15th, 2003, has been described as among the largest coordinated protests in human history. Guinness records the roughly three-million-person rally in Rome as the largest anti-war demonstration on record. Every major American city had one. I remember standing at our local protest in San Diego with my mother and my younger sister. My mother was carrying this enormous sign that said, "Navy Wife for Peace." Television cameras interviewed her with her two little girls alongside. You can sum up much of my life in the contradiction on that sign, because my father was a Navy doctor, and while his wife and daughters were marching against this war, he was already deployed into it. That contradiction became the architecture of my childhood. Our family was raised inside my father's military career. He served honorably and with genuine humanity. And the war, which never should have been executed, was tearing us apart. One deployment, then another, then an extension. I started acting out at school. My grades fell. I remember the crushing sense of responsibility that can settle onto a child who understands far too much and can control absolutely nothing. When he was gone, I would go into my parents' bedroom and put my head on his pillow just to breathe the comfort of his scent. He had one visit home. I remember lying on his chest and crying myself to sleep. I kept a photograph of my parents together in my desk at school. I would sneak looks at it during class. It reminded me of before, before the war, before everything felt like this. Here's something we now know that a nine-year-old watching American television would never have known at the time. Iraq had nothing to do with those attacks. The hijackers, as far as the corporate media told us, were Al-Qaeda, and they were mostly Saudi. Even the strangely composed 9/11 Commission found no evidence that Iraq and Al-Qaeda had developed a collaborative operational relationship and no evidence that Iraq cooperated in planning or carrying out attacks against the United States. The weapons of mass destruction used as a central justification for the invasion were not found. Even America's think tank, the Iraq Survey Group, concluded that Saddam Hussein's nuclear program had ended in 1991 and found no evidence of a serious effort to restart it. That is not what Americans were told in 2002 and 2003. Benjamin Netanyahu came before Congress in September 2002 and told American lawmakers there was "no question whatsoever" Saddam Hussein was pursuing nuclear weapons. He warned that without severe American military action, the terror network would soon have nuclear weapons, too. That lands... differently now. Against the emphatic protest of millions of people in the streets all over the world, including us here at home, America invaded Iraq. I was 11 years old. During those years, I learned a phrase I came to hate, "collateral damage." It's such a bloodless phrase, so self-righteous. It covers so much unnecessary pain. It can mean somebody's child, somebody's mother, somebody's leg, somebody's farm, their home, their school, somebody's entire previous universe of understanding what tomorrow was going to look like. My father was a doctor, and for better or worse, he did not entirely believe in sheltering his eldest daughter from reality. He showed me photographs. His patients were American soldiers and Iraqi civilians, human beings who had encountered shrapnel, explosions, bullets, and kinetic force. After enough violence has been done to a human body, nationality becomes remarkably difficult to determine. That shaped me. Politics was never exactly theoretical after that. War certainly wasn't. Bloody wounds and bereaved loved ones don't argue about how you voted. Folks, it's been 25 years. Let's take stock. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the post-9/11 wars have cost the United States roughly $8 trillion in appropriations and obligations alone, including the long-term cost of caring for wounded veterans. Eight. Trillion. Dollars. That is public wealth, at generational scale, that could have built homes, schools, hospitals, transit, childcare, clean energy, roads, bridges. Could have funded universal healthcare, free college and childcare, reparations, high-speed rail. "Opportunity costs" can sound abstract, so let me be specific. It is the country we did not become. The human ledger is worse. Researchers estimate that more than five million people died in America's major post-9/11 war zones through 2023, both directly from violence, and indirectly from destroyed health systems, malnutrition, disease, wrecked infrastructure, and economic collapse. At least 40 million people were made homeless. At some point, numbers that large almost defeat comprehension. So I come back to one little girl hiding a photograph of her parents in her school desk. Because somewhere in Iraq, there was another child with a similar photograph, and somewhere in Afghanistan, and somewhere in Pakistan, Yemen, Syria, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Iran. In these and many more somewheres, there were mothers trying to explain to a child something that should never have happened and that they did nothing to cause. Let's not forget the war did not remain overseas. The 9/11 attacks were used as a lever to transform American government and society. Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act on October 26th, 2001. The name really is an acronym, U niting and S trengthening A merica by P roviding A ppropriate T ools R equired to I ntercept and O bstruct T errorism. With its passage, the foundations of the modern surveillance state were laid. Americans would never have consented to this intrusive usurpation of our rights and freedoms in a time of peace. For certain agencies and corporations that serve paranoia, it's been an extraordinarily profitable change. Also, the Department of Homeland Security was first created in 2002. Twenty-two agencies were assembled under it in a process taking years. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ICE itself, emerged from that restructuring in 2003. In earlier times, immigration was handled through Labor, not through Security. And some of the changes stayed almost invisible. Shortly after 9/11, USCIS created the Controlled Application Review and Resolution Program, CARRP for short, which the ACLU calls, "Muslims Need Not Apply." Congress, which holds the sole power to make immigration law, declined to authorize this eleven times, but USCIS secretly implemented a special track for immigration applications flagged as national security concerns. Thing is, the criteria they use are, 1, secret, 2, usually innocuous, and 3, unable to ever be challenged or addressed to clear their name. Civil liberties organizations have successfully challenged CARRP in court. It's secretive and discriminatory, particularly toward applicants from Muslim, Arab, Middle Eastern, and South Asian backgrounds. Most Americans have never heard of it. I didn't know about it until a few years ago. My husband, a decorated, disabled US military veteran, has been caught up in it for two decades. These things became part of the institutional architecture of the country we all grew up in. They shaped our lives in countless ways, including the painful and extremely direct through line between Abu Ghraib, which shattered what was left of my innocence, Guantanamo Bay, and modern-day ICE detention. Intelligence agents and soldiers who follow their lead, who are permitted or encouraged to commit war crimes, atrocities, murder, torture, and cruel and unusual punishment in America's name and who face no consequences, continue to climb in their careers, eventually get rotated back home, eventually retire out of the military and join the local police, prison guards, and ICE. The attitude doesn't stay overseas. It comes home to our streets, to our neighborhoods, to our communities. The cruelty, the indifference, the mindset of supremacy, the casual willingness to abuse Black and brown people and justify it in the language of war and self-defense may prove one of the most lasting and consequential harvests of the post-9/11 era, and one that I suspect we'll regret deeply for a very long time to come. And that's what I've spent 25 years trying to understand, because I remember before. I remember singing as a small child, "And I'm proud to be an American, where at least I know I'm free." Meant every word. There was something open-hearted about the patriotism I remember from early childhood. Then the patriotic music... changed. Same flags, same melodies, different emotional register. Something harder entered it, something more frightened, something much less tolerant of dissent. Even the government's instruction to ordinary people felt strange. In the immediate aftermath of the attacks, President Bush told Americans to go shopping. I remember hearing that as a child and thinking, "Really? That's it? That's what citizenship and civic engagement requires of us? Mindless consumption?" My family had taught me something different. My father loved to quote Thomas Paine, "I may not agree with what you have to say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it." My mother sang us a lullaby "Let there be peace on earth, and let it begin with me" Apparently, I took those to heart. Over the years, as my trust in institutions deteriorated, I investigated everything, including the engineering. I've read the official account. I've also read the architects and engineers who have spent two decades arguing that the official account does not fully explain what they saw. They said that the towers came down in ways that resemble controlled demolition more than fire-induced failure. And they point out that Building 7, never struck by a plane, fell in its own footprint at nearly free-fall speed. Now, NIST spent years on this. Its conclusion was fire-induced collapse. I am not an engineer. I'm not going to pretend to adjudicate it. But 25 years later, a substantial number of credentialed professionals still do not find the official explanation adequate. They have petitioned for a new investigation. They have not gotten one. Here's the thing. A nation confident in its own account of a defining catastrophe should not be afraid to answer the questions of its own engineers. Now, distrust is not evidence, but neither is authority. My mother, bless her heart, raised me to question authority and taught me that any legitimate authority would answer you gladly, promptly, and completely. Early on, I believed my country would never lie to me about something this important. Not sure about that anymore. And the fact that I've lost that confidence, that millions of us no longer believe this, is itself one of the profound costs of the last 25 years. I remember President Bush landing on the USS Abraham Lincoln in 2003 beneath that enormous Mission Accomplished banner, claiming that the battles were over and the war was won. In hindsight, I'm pretty sure that was a PR stunt to tell the protesters that we could go home now. The war, of course, had not ended. I was 10, then 11, then 12, at once the child of a deployed military doctor, a victim of family separation, a witness to human suffering, and utterly powerless to change the foreign policy producing it. That complicated moral injury has shaped me in permanent ways. I'm sure I'm not the only one. 25 years later, the progressive destruction of my unquestioning trust in my country has been one of the most painful experiences of my life, and strangely, one of the most liberating. Because patriotism no longer has to mean believing that America has always lived up to its ideals. It can mean deciding that those ideals belong to us, whether our institutions honor them or not. Equality before the law, due process, freedom of conscience, human dignity, government accountable to the people it serves, liberty and justice for all. Those words mattered to the nine-year-old girl I was. They matter more to me now. And that is the accounting I want us to make on this anniversary. Not only who attacked us, truly, not just in media portrayals, but - what did we become afterward? What did we spend and why? Who profited? Whom did we hurt? To whom did we grant impunity or power? What did we surrender? Did we trade essential liberty for temporary safety? Where has that gotten us? What did fear persuade us to tolerate that we never would have accepted before? And what parts of ourselves are we ready to recover? The people murdered on September 11th deserved genuine remembrance, grief unpolluted by the drums of war. The American service members and their families sent into a quarter century of nonstop continuing wars deserved far more than blind nationalistic slogans. The civilians whose countries became battlefields deserve to exist in our accounting at minimum, as they surely deserve to exist in their actual lives. The Muslims and Sikhs and immigrants who discovered that their neighbors or their government suddenly regarded them with suspicion or worse belong in this history too. So do the children waiting for deployed parents to come home, hoping they would, afraid they might not, unable to anticipate how difficult even those homecomings could be. I was one of them, and I remember before. | | ---|---|--- 25 years is long enough to mourn. It is long enough to study, count, pay attention. It's long enough to admit what we got wrong, and it's long enough to decide what lessons we intend to carry into the next 25. For my part, the commitment I made as a child remains remarkably simple. Peace is not the same as passivity. Patriotism is not the same as obedience. And love of country does not require pretending your country is incapable of wrongdoing. It can require exactly the opposite, taking its highest promises seriously enough to hold on to them even when power does not. I'm Melissa Chaudhry. Care, Courage, the Constitution - and the promise I learned before I knew how difficult it would be to keep: liberty and justice for all. The answer is in the numbers. In the March special election, we finished first with 37% of the vote. In the runoff, we came within just 273 votes of winning Paulding County -- a nine-point improvement in a district Donald Trump carried by roughly 37 points. [**Will you chip in $5 today to help us keep organizing in communities the national party has written off?**](http://clicksp.shawnharrisforcongress.com/f/a/4cdnyh18Zypp2lWWgEk_8g~~/AAPPABA~/SctoIEzngSOMeYXF24EyzG2qem2FoL5MaAGnerS3mcRjsv5j5E4CTXLBf2DtKoXgD1hGXwjFBarlwYTpEPep9i0Ue_GWV0JOMF4QnZWKxBRExLASKhYW3wCBQ4_xyNapbp-jlMqzHAeYIeLZdX7tw49IWGqJBy4fNiQPBB4xMyuB47mTbNJPOl9Lffjyg96dysr8NKfTsjJPFc0DDX3rrKYdbBi3RndJn2GEojlydg47MrZ9At6M_FiHjoGsVQlBWcaQN4djlj09Sb6caRKRxI2p3DVnUd5jqqDThAxjqyMpeY_8ZWthIvxCcjwVeujg) That progress did not come from a rescue by Washington. It came from volunteers knocking doors, making calls, holding town halls, and listening to voters who want a representative focused on them. **" When I get to D.C., my focus is one hundred percent you, your kids and your grandkids."** That is the kind of campaign we are building: local, accountable, and powered by people who believe this district deserves better than Trump-endorsed Clay Fuller. They wrote this district off, but voters are proving them wrong. But narrowing the gap is not enough. We have to close it, and that takes a field program strong enough to reach every persuadable voter across GA-14. [**Please donate $3 or whatever you can today to help us put more organizers on the ground and finish what we started.**](http://clicksp.shawnharrisforcongress.com/f/a/4cdnyh18Zypp2lWWgEk_8g~~/AAPPABA~/SctoIEzngSOMeYXF24EyzG2qem2FoL5MaAGnerS3mcRjsv5j5E4CTXLBf2DtKoXgD1hGXwjFBarlwYTpEPep9i0Ue_GWV0JOMF4QnZWKxBRExLASKhYW3wCBQ4_xyNapbp-jlMqzHAeYIeLZdX7tw49IWGqJBy4fNiQPBB4xMyuB47mTbNJPOl9Lffjyg96dysr8NKfTsjJPFc0DDX3rrKYdbBi3RndJn2GEojlydg47MrZ9At6M_FiHjoGsVQlBWcaQN4djlj09Sb6caRKRxI2p3DVnUd5jqqDThAxjqyMpeY_8ZWthIvxCcjwVeujg)

| | | Peter, It has been 25 years since an ordinary September morning became a day that none of us will ever forget.
I remember sitting in our legislative offices at the U.S. Capitol. I remember immediately knowing something was amiss after the first plane. I remember seeing the second plane and having my worst fears confirmed - America was under attack. I remember the alarms and evacuating the Rayburn House Office Building as the Pentagon was being hit, believing the Capitol was next. I remember the fear, the confusion, the fighter jets flying overhead, the mass of people fleeing our U.S. Capitol.

2,977 individuals lost their lives on that fateful day.
What I also remember is how Americans responded.
Police, firefighters and first responders ran toward the danger. They bravely entered the buildings, climbed the stairs and went where they were needed. That’s what heroes do.
Passengers on Flight 93 stood together and said “Let’s Roll!” before courageously fighting back. They sacrificed their lives to save thousands of others - possibly my own. That’s what selfless leaders do.
People stopped to provide comfort, shelter and care to complete strangers. Everyone prayed for and rallied around anyone who needed some love. That’s what neighbors do.
Everyone across the country rallied behind our president, our troops and proudly flew our flag. Partisan politics didn’t matter...people did. We united in the common cause of liberty. That is what Americans do.
We will never be able to replace those we lost. We will never be able to repay the brave men and women who courageously responded, stood up and led. But we can honor them by serving and protecting the country they left us. In fact, I believe we have a solemn duty to do so.
Between now and November, I am asking my fellow Tennesseans to make the effort to understand the issues, get to know the candidates, ask the tough questions, and volunteer. Importantly, **I am asking everyone to vote.**
Our republic is ours to serve, and our neighbors are ours to serve and protect.
Most of us will never be asked to make the type of sacrifices made by those brave souls 25 years ago. But we should all expect each other to care enough to show up, participate and leave this country better than we found it.
May God bless everyone who lost a loved one or friend on September 11th. May God bless every first responder and service member who answered the call. May God bless all of us who are still haunted by the memories of that dark day. May God bless this beautiful country we call home.
Chairman John Ray Clemmons

Peter,
Trump's unprecedented "midterm convention" just wrapped up and it was one of the most sad, pathetic, and dark political events in recent history.
Here are just some of the highlights of the event:

* There were tens of thousands of empty seats in the arena.

* Trump tried to bribe voters by promising $5,000 checks for every American if MAGA wins this November.

* During a speech by Ted Cruz, an audience member shouted "he should be shot" three times at the mention of Zohran Mamdani, James Talarico, and Abdul El-Sayed. Ted Cruz refused to condemn it.

* JD Vance said in his speech: "Because Democrats have become such a nightmare, we can never, will never let them win."

* Trump ordered the audience to raise their right hand, had them proclaim he was the "greatest president ever" and pledge to "cheat like hell" in the upcoming midterm elections.

The convention was darkly reminiscent of the Nazi Party's infamous Nuremberg Rallies. It also reeked of desperation--the last, violent gasps of a dying fascist movement. MAGA has made it clear they won't go quietly. They'll lie, cheat, threaten, anything and everything to win this November.
The November election will be one of the most consequential turning points in American history. We either let Trump cheat to cement his fascist takeover of America, or we smoother MAGA and turn the page on one of the darkest chapters in American history.
We choose the latter, and that's why Defend Our Courts is leading the charge to put MAGA down for good. We're fighting to expand the firewall of state Supreme Courts, the courts that can prevent Trump's election rigging, on a national scale, while turning out voters in states with key House and Senate races.
But it's going to take a ton of resources to operate on the scale this moment demands. Folks, it’s James Carville.

I’ve spent nearly half a century helping Democrats win elections, and I’m gonna tell you something plainly:

**For too long, we have waited until the house was already on fire before deciding to buy a hose.**

We wait until a race becomes a crisis.

We wait until a great candidate is getting buried in attack ads.

We wait until Republicans have already built the infrastructure, raised the money, and defined the battlefield.

Then everybody starts running around asking what happened.

Well, Raja Krishnamoorthi has gone and done something about it.

He founded [**Equal Opportunity Now**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139024671/645968160/1090555623?refcode=260911_carville_resend&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDUvMS83MzE2OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMjBlNDA4OS0xNWFlLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=khyfYDu2ji48XaWBEgox_82uKuv4-cz96KlNRnW3a-A=) to find and support bold leaders and important causes before it’s too late — leaders who will stand up to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement, fight for working families, and actually deliver results.

And all I can say is:

**FINALLY.**

Finally, an organization that understands we cannot defeat MAGA with timid candidates, stale talking points, and a last-minute panic.

But Raja cannot build this by himself.

[**Will you contribute $25, $50, or whatever you can today to help Equal Opportunity Now find, fund, and support the leaders Democrats need to start winning again?**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139024672/645968161/1090555623?refcode=260911_carville_resend&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDUvMS83MzE2OSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMjBlNDA4OS0xNWFlLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=khyfYDu2ji48XaWBEgox_82uKuv4-cz96KlNRnW3a-A=)

Now, I know Raja.
He is smart. He is tough. And he knows firsthand what opportunity can mean.
His family came to this country with very little. They relied on public housing and food stamps. He worked his way from Peoria all the way to Congress.
And instead of pulling the ladder up behind him, Raja has spent his career fighting to make sure the next family gets the same shot.
That means standing up for workers.
Holding powerful corporations and corrupt politicians accountable.
Defending immigrants, voting rights, and every American targeted by Trump’s politics of division.
And now he is putting that experience toward building the next generation of Democratic leadership.
**Here’s the truth: The leaders we need are already out there.**
They are running for city council, state legislature, Congress, and offices most national donors are not paying attention to yet.
They have the courage.
They have the ideas.
What they do not always have is the money, infrastructure, and early support necessary to compete.
That is where Equal Opportunity Now comes in.

clean_body: I’ve spent nearly half a century helping Democrats win elections, and I’m gonna tell you something plainly: | | | | | | | = Folks, it’s James Carville. I’ve spent nearly half a century helping Democrats win elections, and I’m gonna tell you something plainly: For too long, we have waited until the house was already on fire before deciding to buy a hose. We wait until a race becomes a crisis. We wait until a great candidate is getting buried in attack ads. We wait until Republicans have already built the infrastructure, raised the money, and defined the battlefield. Then everybody starts running around asking what happened. Well, Raja Krishnamoorthi has gone and done something about it. He founded = to find and support bold leaders and important causes before it’s too late — leaders who will stand up to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement, fight for working families, and actually deliver results. And all I can say is: FINALLY. Finally, an organization that understands we cannot defeat MAGA with timid candidates, stale talking points, and a last-minute panic. But Raja cannot build this by himself. = = | | | = Now, I know Raja. He is smart. He is tough. And he knows firsthand what opportunity can mean. His family came to this country with very little. They relied on public housing and food stamps. He worked his way from Peoria all the way to Congress. And instead of pulling the ladder up behind him, Raja has spent his career fighting to make sure the next family gets the same shot. That means standing up for workers. Holding powerful corporations and corrupt politicians accountable. Defending immigrants, voting rights, and every American targeted by Trump’s politics of division. And now he is putting that experience toward building the next generation of Democratic leadership. Here’s the truth: The leaders we need are already out there. They are running for city council, state legislature, Congress, and offices most national donors are not paying attention to yet. They have the courage. They have the ideas. What they do not always have is the money, infrastructure, and early support necessary to compete. That is where Equal Opportunity Now comes in. = = We’ve got a good battle plan, now, let’s help Raja build this damn thing. \-- James Carville | = Equal Opportunity Now is d/b/a Reviving American Jobs Again PAC (RAJA PAC) Equal Opportunity Now P.O. Are we the America that chooses to protect, serve, and celebrate one another? The America that champions science – that draws on the world’s most brilliant minds to solve the insolvable? The America that leads the world in doing what’s right, even if it’s hard? I know the America I’m fighting for – the one I’ve fought for since I had my first taste of civil disobedience back in the 60s. I’m asking you to join me.= The truth is that this moment in history feels like no other. So I have to ask: what would you give to stop this? **North Carolina is the best chance Democrats have to flip a Republican-held Senate seat this November.** You don’t have to just take our word for it, though – all of the experts agree:

**With national Republicans spending nearly $100 million so far to defeat him, the only way he’ll be able to overcome their attacks and surge ahead is with help from grassroots supporters like you.**
[**_Your first contribution of $5 now will go a long way toward ensuring Roy wins in November and Democrats take back the Senate. _This was the fall of 2001. I was 21, three months out of college,

had left stains ground into the carpet, and I was still working on

Tuesday, and I was in the South, nowhere near New York._

_A petition before an unelected wildlife commission could ban the lead
ammunition used to hunt nearly every legal game species in Colorado._

*
A BACKDOOR BAN ON HUNTING: The petition, filed by 18 organizations
tied to former Humane Society leader Wayne Pacelle, would make it
illegal to possess traditional lead ammunition or any firearm capable
of firing it while hunting elk, deer, bear, turkey and more.

*
AN UNELECTED COMMISSION HOLDS THE POWER: The Colorado Parks and
Wildlife Commission's 11 members are appointed by Gov. Jared Polis and
confirmed by the Senate, meaning voters have no direct say over
regulations that could reshape hunting, ranching and gun ownership
statewide.

*
RANCHERS COULD PAY THE PRICE TOO: A related petition would ban prairie
dog shooting on public and CPW-controlled land, and the author warns
that could push expanding prairie dog colonies onto private ranchland,
leaving landowners to absorb the damage.

# **[$800,000 a day is the new price of sailing past Iran](https://substack.com/redirect/094a49f4-a49f-4766-ad99-3e0782abf35d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Baltic Middle East-to-China VLCC rates just printed $800,000 a day after U.S. forces wrecked five Iranian-linked tankers. Crude is still moving. The invoice is not. U.S. Gulf-to-Asia now costs $29.5 million a voyage, $15 a barrel before war-risk. In **["The Iran deal and the Space X IPO"](https://substack.com/redirect/5dbd99d9-6729-430e-a333-9160c97f8b16?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** I said the Hormuz premium got vaporized temporarily. That pause just died.
* **Winners?** VLCC owners, two-year lessors, and war-risk desks. Kpler keeps earnings above $100,000 a day into early next year. Morgan Stanley sees leases jumping another 20% to 30%.
* **Losers?** Asian refiners eating $15 a barrel freight, pump buyers, and every central bank fighting imported inflation. Iran's shadow fleet is now target practice and a rate spike.
* **Next?** Rates stay bid. The Gulf of Oman-to-East Asia benchmark is already up 85% to almost $386,000 a day. Ship-to-ship transfers keep barrels moving. Hormuz is a tax, not a shutdown.

Vitol says 10 million barrels a day still cross. Goldman says 15 million. Volume is not the story. Transit is. HPCL-Mittal already said it: the crude is there, the ships are the choke. Freight inflation stacks on crude inflation and lands on gasoline, diesel, and store shelves. Short the peace. Long the boats.

# **[Coinbase already priced a Clarity Act failure and kept selling](https://substack.com/redirect/094a49f4-a49f-4766-ad99-3e0782abf35d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Senate cloture on the Clarity Act hits September 15. Senator Lummis says if this Congress blows it, the next real window is 2030. Coinbase CFO Alesia Haas told Goldman she never bet the firm on one vote. Three paths: Congress, the agencies, or the courts. Fail the floor, and she launches through Atkins at the SEC and Selig at the CFTC anyway.
* **Winners?** Coinbase either way. Congress is the rocket. Agency rulemaking is the grind. Compliant exchanges that already built the stack collect sideline capital first.
* **Losers?** Anyone who treated September 15 as binary for the entire U.S. crypto complex. Offshore cowboys if America stays in the fog. Idle cash that needed a statute before it would move.
* **Next?** Cloture is the tape. Fail, and Lummis's 2030 clock starts. Haas still ships via Atkins and Selig. Clarity speeds sideline money. It does not invent the business.

This is not bravery. This is optionality. Coinbase spent years leaning into regulation so a Senate procedural vote cannot kill the roadmap. The stock was up 1.34% while they said the quiet part out loud. The industry wanted a law. The CFO bought three exits. September 15 decides the speed. It does not decide whether Coinbase keeps selling.

_9/11 25th Anniversary – 25 Years of Remembrance_
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139028566/645981165/1228991292?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDMvMS82NzYzNSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkM2UyZGE4OC0yNGFlLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogIkRQV0lMTElTNjdAR01BSUwuQ09NIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=UA3QL5XJwzSwZvDwoZidH9Jq_xexlxKFLdfOd6tgyJU=&emci=f183f928-1aae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=d3e2da88-24ae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=4925535) Today marks 25 years since the attacks on September 11, 2001. We remember the nearly 3,000 lives lost that day. We honor the firefighters, police officers, and first responders who acted bravely and selflessly. We will always remember the lives lost, the sacrifices made, and the lasting impact – over 6,000 Americans have lost their lives due to 9/11 exposure in the years since the attacks. Hoosiers, like all Americans, will never forget. ****
_Hoosier Families are Being Denied SNAP Replacement Benefits After Losing Power for Two Weeks_
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139028567/645981166/432802826?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDMvMS82NzYzNSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkM2UyZGE4OC0yNGFlLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogIkRQV0lMTElTNjdAR01BSUwuQ09NIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=UA3QL5XJwzSwZvDwoZidH9Jq_xexlxKFLdfOd6tgyJU=&emci=f183f928-1aae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=d3e2da88-24ae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=4925535) After the August storms caused Indiana Northwest communities to lose power for over two weeks, they’re still facing unfair punishment, this time from their own state government. The state is only approving replacements for households that received their monthly benefits before August 11, and some of those Hoosiers were denied as well.. Legal advocates say that this policy is out-of-step with federal law. If Braun wanted to, he could issue blanket replacement benefits for the whole area impacted. There is no reason for this arbitrary restriction other than Republicans constant efforts to punish those who are most in need. _Each week, the State Party will highlight key policy or programs from Democrats at the Statehouse or across the state. Democrats deliver a better future for Hoosier families, and we urge you to share this information with your networks._ _Indiana Supreme Court Overrules Recount Commission, Demands Ballots Be Counted Where Voters Did Nothing Wrong_
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/139028568/645981167/1902587900?nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMDMvMS82NzYzNSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkM2UyZGE4OC0yNGFlLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogIkRQV0lMTElTNjdAR01BSUwuQ09NIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=UA3QL5XJwzSwZvDwoZidH9Jq_xexlxKFLdfOd6tgyJU=&emci=f183f928-1aae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=d3e2da88-24ae-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=4925535) On Thursday, Hoosier voters got a big victory. The Indiana Supreme Court ruled that six ballots that were tossed out in the State Senate District 23 Republican Primary must be counted. This means anti-redistricting State Senator Spencer Deery will prevail over Trump-endorsed challenger Paula Copenhaver. Indiana Republicans, including Max Engling and Diego Morales, wanted to throw away legally cast votes by Hoosier citizens because of small, administrative errors by their own Party’s county clerks. The State Supreme Court had the final say – and it’s a win for every voter. # **RPVI Endorses Derrick Callwood for Senate**
---

| |

Dear Friends,
Last week, we introduced Eric Tillett and shared the plans he is bringing to voters across the Virgin Islands.
**Today, the Republican Party in the Virgin Islands is proud to endorse Derrick Callwood for Senate in the St. Thomas–St. John District.**
A proud St. Thomas resident, Derrick is a former Virgin Islands police officer and local businessman. His background has given him a practical perspective on public safety, the pressures facing local businesses, and the consequences when government fails to perform. He is running to bring real opposition, real oversight, and real accountability to the Legislature.
Derrick’s priorities begin with problems Virgin Islanders confront every day: corruption, WAPA, community safety, education, the cost of living, and access to affordable healthcare. One example is his call to replace WAPA’s failed model and impose real oversight so residents can have reliable power and lower costs, not more debt and excuses.
That is the kind of direct accountability our Legislature needs.
For nearly three decades, the Legislature has operated without a single Republican member. Electing Derrick will provide a voice in the Senate willing to expose problems, challenge business as usual, and demand answers when government fails.
We invite you to read our new profile of Derrick and learn more about the experience, priorities, and commitment to accountability he would bring to the Legislature.
---
| [LEARN MORE ABOUT DERRICK ](https://us.list-manage.com/Th_eu0K8viW?e=4f81ceec6f&c2id=39a671a1d75d16cde42206c3cb925b2d)
---
| |
More competition means more accountability, which creates a better government for all of us.
Onward!John Yob
Chairman

A Chinese national who worked as a U.S. Customs and Border Protection supervisor in Calais was arrested after FBI agents said he altered computers at three Maine border facilities. Kennedy accused Gov. Josh Shapiro’s administration of making them up. He then reportedly pushed the CDC to remove those deaths from its national tally. **That is an abuse of power that puts our communities at risk.** And now we know Kennedy was not truthful with Congress about his record, either. He repeatedly claimed his 2019 trip to Samoa had “nothing to do with vaccines,” but newly uncovered documents show he proposed assessing the country’s MMR vaccines before the trip. Months later, Samoa suffered a devastating measles outbreak that killed 83 people, including 72 young children. **RFK Jr. has shown what he will do with power when no one stops him. Unfortunately, this is nothing new for Republicans. In fact, they are opening up their old playbook — purging voters from the rolls to hold on to their power.
More than a million Texans have been placed on “voter suspense” lists, forcing them to update their voter registration status or face ineligibility to vote this year.
Meanwhile, Tarrant County has announced plans to slash the number of polling places where people can vote, which will result in longer lines, lower turnout, and confusion among voters.
Peter, we can’t let Republicans keep getting away with these voter suppression and intimidation tactics. We’ve got to get the word out to Texas voters and ensure they show up in such big numbers that we overwhelm the GOP anti-voter crusade. Headlines like these can be discouraging at first, but for me they’re a call to action. A call to keep backing the next generation of democratic fighters who will fight tooth and nail to stop these kinds of attacks on our rights before they ever get off the ground.
We are supporting several young progressive candidates in Texas, including **Kristian Carranza** , **Julio Salinas** , and **Tyler Smith** , all of whom represent the very best of the next generation of leaders. They refuse to take corporate cash, relying instead on grassroots support to fund their campaigns. And that means that they need people like you to help them face down voter suppression and win.

## Born Without Arms, Chasing Le Mans
Callum Smith fell in love with motorsport at 2 years old, watching bike racing with his grandad. Born without arms, he grew up using his feet for everything: writing, eating with a knife and fork, playing guitar, and gaming on Xbox. ## Alzheimer's Patient Regains Memory, Finds Love
Gail Youngdale, a Texas woman living with Alzheimer's disease, says she has regained most of her memory after years of uncertainty. And that's not the only second chance she's celebrating. "_I don't have all of my memory back, but most of it_ ," [Gail said](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LEOmzAYBOCngc0I_wkYDx6yoAylQ5eMyJjf8LfGjmwHRJ6-oq_Q_XT67l7DOGhy5JefekNlFztmG0aPR3KYM8bRfpwzFI1DF3ZMOaJf8krej1BDy2rJOB-1ybTj2JSzsoiAtxIVF53k7f1-E-WqJsknCa2euJUodKNBYIfCCuiMtqYpSV11teQcoBa8raSY0TQcwJhuAiuKe40z5RCr34F8XtG6M-wYKxO20qk153cqbo8C-gL64ziq9PH-TH_O75UooF9CmNk1rIC-BdkW0L_Cpj17UV7Zw31XpA0jS-wXLpp8YkNImQXLnhjZgFuIJ-vJz4n9CDsy7Wf2DG8so5rfBzlHqb2Uy6bJ_VPl__9zV_A3AAD__yMXjkY). Just a few years ago, Gail's Alzheimer's was progressing. Brain scans showed nine areas of amyloid plaque, and daily life had become filled with anxiety and uncertainty for her family. Gail began receiving what was then an experimental Alzheimer's drug that targets amyloid in the brain. After undergoing treatment, her daughter says [scans no longer show the plaque](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkDGynDAQRE8jMm1JAx-WQIETZd-pQ2oQA4wtJCzNX2p9ehe-guOu6n79fnxOn8iR0_YdD3Lrtk6y5inRVSOJUJnWrxgDlxAp5hdVKZQ22TmlCQz02oza2gmD8Iumj2ZxKxFQ25Czw3O0fde1Q7M7mM3QdrM1o-lwmZc-AHYtEXRziziaht1dZ0ZrAcxg-8c4LBQ-LEAIzxnWQXWGFpZcHj8zJ9lpje_8ovII-Wii20XOqtpvCrwCf13X41dFuUMF_r6jwMccMCrw95ICb54KfGsVeIx_duKDStUnClMSfe1ZV7z0XJCTPiP-_iK9cMXzJCy67lio6iq5vDUnnVA4J4w64HEib0mBb4pbzotj5Nrf-NuBHP_hyv-Lfjn4GwAA___hrZYF). body:

place my American flag stamps upside down.

Patriot,

When I’m writing thank-you notes to donors, I very intentionally
place my American flag stamps upside down.

[Envelope with upside down flag stamp]
[https://link.email.america1stwarroom.com/click/e11674331/UaHR0cHM6Ly9zZWN1cmUuYW5lZG90LmNvbS9zdGFuZC1pbi10aGUtZ2FwL3NiLWFjdGlvbi8/SZW1haWxfYW1lcmljYU9ORXN0d2Fycm9vbV9jb20yNjA5MTE/LbmNsV0dLQ015WQ/qP3V0bV9jYW1wYWlnbj1zaXRnMjYwODEyJnV0bV9tZWRpdW09cmV2c2hhcmUmdXRtX3NvdXJjZT1zYiZ1dG1fdGVybT0yMzU4MV93cjEmdXRtX2NvbnRlbnQ9aW1hZ2UxXQ/gaqR_Cw/s3g310d8900

I’m not sure if you’re aware of this, but it symbolizes a
“citizen in distress”.

When the J6ers were in prison and wrote letters to supporters and
anyone on the outside, we would place our stamps upside down to let
them know how we were being treated, in case our messages were being
censored.

I CONTINUE TO USE IT BECAUSE IT SYMBOLIZES HOW J6ERS ARE STILL IN
DISTRESS.

Even though we’ve been pardoned, many of us are still trying to
rebuild from the ground up. There are some who are in need of jobs,
reliable transportation, housing, help paying utilities, food, and
support for their families.

That’s why Stand in the Gap Foundation exists.

Through emergency financial assistance, practical resources, donated
vehicles, and compassionate support, we give these men and women a

subject: With justice for all

body:
[ https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/go/892?refcode=em20260911-6711-footer&t=1001&akid=6711%2E420207%2EZN9PcL ]Pramila Jayapal

Peter,

In the aftermath of 9/11, prejudice against immigrant communities was at
an all-time high – so I did something about it. I founded OneAmerica
(originally Hate Free Zone) to bring immigrants together and organize for
our rights.

Yesterday, 25 years and two wonderful executive directors later, I joined
OneAmerica Votes to speak out again. This time on the Trump
administration’s attacks on immigrant communities. To do something about
it, together.

Today, I’m sharing my words with you:

On September 21, 2002, 14-year-old Mohamed Hamoui testified at
OneAmerica’s Justice for All townhall:

“On February 22, 2002, something happened that I never thought possible;
after all, this is America. At 7 a.m. that morning, seven...agents dragged
my parents and sister out of bed with guns and flashlights...Since then,
they have all been suffering in detention.”

This was a landmark public hearing organized by OneAmerica, bringing
immigrants targeted by the post-9/11 crackdown to testify in the face of
enormous personal safety concerns.

Our hearing made a difference. And we were called to organize again. This
time for the U.S. Senate, gathering immigrants from across the country to
testify.

With this push we successfully sued the Bush Administration, preventing
the deportations of more than 4,000 Somali immigrants.

OneAmerica has been at the forefront of every major fight for immigrant
rights in Washington state, growing and building people power — for us, by
us — to strengthen our movement.

Even as the Trump Administration continuously tries to take us backwards,
we have grown stronger — the coordination across communities has
increased, the tactics and strategies have solidified, and new leaders
continue to emerge.

Though we know this moment remains terrifying. We have witnessed horrors
in Minnesota, in Chicago, and right here in Washington state, as people
are kidnapped by masked agents, unable to contact their families until
they’ve already been taken halfway across the country.

We are witnessing in real time the destruction of legal pathways and a
complete disregard for due process.

But even since the earliest days at Hate Free Zone, I have seen time and
time again strength and courage emerging in times of crisis. When we dig
deep, we find new resources, new leaders, new allies, new strategies, and
a new level of commitment to justice that remains stronger than their
cruelty.

OneAmerica has grown in remarkable ways — including through OneAmerica
Votes. Those investments are paying off as we build the bench of leaders
inside and outside elected office to ensure that Washington state remains
one of the most immigrant-friendly states in the country.

This is the theory of change that first got me into elected office: that
we need organizers on the inside and the outside to change how politics is
done.

To develop legislation with our communities. To demand more from elected
officials. To build new coalitions that cut across race, class, gender,
and national origin and focus on the values we all share.

In the moments that are most painful, where it seems like we have taken so
many steps backwards — look at how much has been built.

Look at the rejection of Donald Trump and his hateful anti-immigrant
actions by the American people. Look at the rise of a powerful new energy,
of diverse leaders demanding a different kind of politics that requires
real, humane immigration reform and refuses to back down until we get it.

And that will propel us to taking back the House in November, at which
point I intend to haul in each and every one of these corrupt Trump
officials before the Immigration Subcommittee and demand accountability as
we continue to fight for a just immigration system.

What an honor it is to have founded OneAmerica 25 years ago, but what an
even bigger honor it's been to see it grow and lead in new beautiful,
strategic, loving ways — towards justice for all.

[ https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/sign/em20260911-oneamerica-petition/?source=em20260911-6711&t=1002&akid=6711%2E420207%2EZN9PcL ]Peter, will
you add your name to stand with me in the fight to secure a better future
for all of us?

[ https://act.pramilaforcongress.com/sign/em20260911-oneamerica-petition/?source=em20260911-6711&t=1003&akid=6711%2E420207%2EZN9PcL ]Add Your Name

Thank you,

Pramila Jayapal

The South Dakota State Fair Governor’s Debate, Hosted by Farmers Union

When I stepped onto the Freedom Stage at the State Fair in Huron, I was prepared to speak for the hundreds of South Dakotans I’ve met on the campaign trail. When I stepped off, I realized that Governor Rhoden truly believes that things are just fine.

But this isn’t the story I’m hearing from South Dakotans.

Access to healthcare in small rural communities is declining. The number of young South Dakotan farmers seeing a future in our state is dwindling. Our rural schools are struggling, and farmers have to foot the bill. Our elected officials are standing in the way of ballot measures and attacking popular initiatives. I don’t see what Governor Rhoden is seeing, and neither do South Dakotans.

Investing in agricultural incubators and leasing incentives is how we create opportunities for new markets. Proactively supporting the Governor’s Housing Program is how we give struggling South Dakotans the opportunity to grow roots. Supporting products that come from our own ranchers and farmers – instead of out of state businesses and foreign companies – is how we strengthen our economy. What we need is leadership that believes in coming together to get to work and has the confidence to depart from the status quo. That’s what I’m here for.

I’m incredibly grateful to the Farmers Union for moderating and organizing such a great event. You can access the full debate using the link below, along with the coverage by Dakota News Now.

| | | [Watch it here!](https://us.list-manage.com/j6eBGhJkYBE?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)
---
| | | [Dakota News Now Article](https://us.list-manage.com/FOnJX3fd7xH?e=cee7b49c04&c2id=3adc23449cf80dcda430cceaf3c4b05d)
---
| | | |
---
| |
---
Conversations in Rapid City

While I was in Rapid City, I had the opportunity to be a part of several community gatherings. United Way held an incredibly insightful information session about Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed (ALICE) working families. ALICE working families earn more than the federal poverty level, but still struggle to afford basic everyday needs. I learned a lot from the experts and the perspectives that this event platformed. Raising awareness about ways to support struggling families and individuals from a variety of backgrounds is something I will always support and be a part of. Everyone deserves the resources they need to live life comfortably and to the fullest without constantly worrying about putting food on the table or making it to the next paycheck.

I also got to meet with a local group called Wingnuts, where I listened to their concerns about property rights, transparency, and government accountability. Before hitting the road, I ended my day by attending a town hall in Main Street Square, where I shared the pillars of my campaign with others and answered questions. I’m incredibly grateful to each and every community, organization, and individual that made time to speak with me.

| | |
---
| |
---
Voices in the Middle

I’d like to thank the Sioux Falls folks at Voices in the Middle for giving me the opportunity to listen to South Dakotans, and to share my vision for the future of South Dakota. Voices in the Middle is dedicated to political engagement that is inclusive and prioritizes productive conversation.

Folks brought me concerns about the lack of support for education and educators and about the state’s failure to meet funding requirements – despite having a large surplus, year after year. The role of the government is to invest in the resources that you need. Citizens vote to have control over government spending and to have access to vital services. Your tax dollars should be used to make your life better – not to collect dust in our reserves. This isn’t fiscal responsibility. It’s making the appearance of responsibility, while failing to meet the actual funding responsibilities that our state has commited to South Dakotans.

Building coalitions, providing accessible leadership, and inspiring creative solutions to our state’s problems is what my campaign is all about; being a part of events like this one is just one example of how listening and showing up leads to positive change for everyone.
