Huron, Town Hall: 9/14, 7-8 p.m.

Aberdeen, Northern State Townhall: 9/17, 5-7 p.m., Barnett Center

Four more years of Republican rule will get South Dakota nowhere.

I have the change we need.

# [America Was Not Built on Fear](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=6380051&post_id=215293300&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjE1MjkzMzAwLCJpYXQiOjE3ODkxNjYyOTAsImV4cCI6MTc5MTc1ODI5MCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTYzODAwNTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.r5HPYYyDewk-6oDqdjDBlmEy1qy-MMPYgz_tnY6v3sg)

---
| | [READ IN APP](https://open.substack.com/pub/haleyformi/p/america-was-not-built-on-fear?utm_source=email&redirect=app-store-no-desktop&inbox=true&utm_campaign=email-read-in-app)
---

On January 8, 1947, President Harry Truman stood before Congress and said seven words that have outlived the moment in which he spoke them:
**" America was not built on fear."**
America, Truman said, was built "on courage, on imagination and an unbeatable determination to do the job at hand."
I have been thinking about those words today.
Because twenty-five years ago, America had every reason to be afraid.
The sky over New York filled with smoke. A plane struck the Pentagon. Another fell into a field in Pennsylvania.
And 2,977 people who woke up on an ordinary Tuesday morning never came home.
They were parents children. Husbands and wives. Brothers and sisters. Coworkers and friends.
They had meetings on their calendars. Dinner plans that night. Birthdays coming. Children waiting to be picked up from school.
And then, in 102 minutes, the world changed changed.
We often remember September 11 because of what was taken from us.
But twenty-five years later, I also think we should remember what was revealed about us.
America was attacked. Americans also went to work. And on one of the darkest mornings in our history, ordinary Americans reminded the world what those stars and stripes mean.
Firefighters climbed the stairs while everyone else was coming down.
Police officers ran toward the smoke.
Paramedics and first responders moved toward danger because there were people on the other side of it who needed them.
Passengers aboard Flight 93, confronted with the unimaginable, acted together.
Strangers reached for strangers.
People carried people whose names they would never know.
That was courage. But it was also something simpler.
There was a job at hand. And Americans did it.
I represent Michigan. I come from a state where we know something about doing the job at hand.
We build things. We fix things. We work shifts. We solve problems.
And when something breaks, the people I know, don't have much patience for standing around arguing about who gets credit for picking up the wrench.
You pick it up.
You get to work.
You take care of the person next to you.
And you don't quit until the job is done.
There is something deeply American about that.
It's in the factory worker reporting for the early shift. It's in the firefighter putting on the helmet. It's in the police officer answering the call. It's in the servicemember raising a hand and taking an oath.
Different uniforms. Different jobs.
Same promise: When the call comes, Americans show up.
Standing alongside law enforcement and public servants at the 9/11 memorial in Michigan today, looking at the wreaths and the names and the uniforms, you're reminded how inadequate so many of the categories we use to divide ourselves can become.
We were never supposed to be identical.
We were supposed to be **one**.
There is a difference.
Because a wreath doesn't ask how you voted.
A uniform doesn't ask where you came from.
A name carved into a memorial doesn't tell you which arguments somebody won.
It tells you that somebody was here.
That somebody was loved.
That somebody served.
That somebody mattered.
And suddenly the things that seemed enormous yesterday become very small.
And every once in a while, history gives us a moment that strips everything else away and reminds humanity of the things that belong to all of us.
September 11 is one of those moments.
The grief belongs to all of us.
The gratitude belongs to all of us.
The responsibility to remember belongs to all of us.
And the flag belongs to all of us.
That is why twenty-five years matters.
An entire generation of Americans now knows September 11 not as a memory, but as history. The National September 11 Memorial & Museum estimates that roughly 100 million Americans are now too young to remember that day themselves which makes remembering more important, not less.
Because memory isn't simply about looking backward, it's the promise of what we need to carry forward. And that responsibility belongs to all of us.
So we will tell them about the firefighters climbing, about the officers running toward the smoke, about the passengers who fought back, about the people who lined up to give blood, about the flags hanging from porches.
We will tell them how on one of the darkest days in our history, Americans looked at one another and understood, without needing to be told:
_You 're my neighbor._
_You 're my countryman._
_You 're not facing this alone._
That is part of the story of September 11, too.
And perhaps that is the part we are most responsible for carrying forward.
Because patriotism isn't only remembering what happened to America.
It's remembering what America is supposed to be.
A country confident enough to be free.
Strong enough to be generous.
Brave enough to run toward the fire.
And stubborn enough, when something is broken, to pick up the wrench and get to work.
Harry Truman said America was not built on fear.
Twenty-five years ago, fear came to our shores.
And Americans answered it with courage.
With service.
With sacrifice.
And with an unbeatable determination to do the job at hand.
Today, we remember the 2,977 lives stolen on September 11, 2001. We honor the heroes who ran toward danger. We hold close the families who have spent a quarter century living with an empty chair, a missing voice, a birthday that arrives every year without the person who should be there.
And we make them a promise.
We will remember not only how they died.
But we also remember our country answered.
How we served.
How we sacrificed.
How we showed up for one another.
**America was not built on fear.**
It was built by people who showed up.
And it still is.
And may we never, ever, forget it.

We’re aiming to knock 5,000 doors across 70 canvasses next weekend.
#
Hi there,
Z here, Voter Contact Director at Swing Left! I’m reaching out about our upcoming Weekend of Action on September 19th and 20th.
**We’re aiming to knock 5,000 doors across 70 canvasses, and we still need more canvass hosts and volunteers to help us make it happen.**
In total, we’re working to have hundreds of thousands of conversations with voters by Election Day—and it’s going to take all of us doing what we can to reach that goal.
**If you’d like to be a part of our upcoming Weekend of Action, there are two different ways to take action today:**
1. [**You can host a canvass to talk with voters in the swing districts and states we need to win this November.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2361?utm_source=em20260911-2751&t=1&akid=2751%2E1562180%2EZXtsuz)

2. [**Or, you can sign up to join us Saturday for a canvass training, get the tools you need, and be assigned a set of doors to knock in a Swing Left target race during the Weekend of Action.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/2362?utm_source=em20260911-2751&t=2&akid=2751%2E1562180%2EZXtsuz)

With just over 7 weeks until Election Day, every conversation each of us has on the doors will help build the relationships and organizing power Democrats need to flip the House and Senate. So please join us in whatever way works best for you!
Hope to see you out there,
Z Mooney
Voter Contact Director, Swing Left
P.S. Don’t live near a swing district or state? [**You can make calls from the comfort of your home to connect with voters in high-stakes swing districts nationwide.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/499?utm_source=em20260911-2751&t=3&akid=2751%2E1562180%2EZXtsuz)

**Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power.** Right now, Swing Left is investing in grassroots organizing in key swing districts and initiatives across the country to flip the House and win the Senate and critical states in 2026. [**If you’d like to help support our work, you can make a donation using this link.**](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em_ms_sl_footer?refcode=em20260911-1&t=4&refcode2=2751_1562180_ZXtsuz&akid=2751%2E1562180%2EZXtsuz)

_**Cliff 's Note:**_
##### I have written about September 11 before, in pieces. I had never told it all the way through, and this morning, twenty-five years on, I decided to, on camera, for whoever showed up. Nearly three hundred of you did, without an email, and I am grateful.
##### This is not a rant. It is what I saw from a street corner on the Lower East Side, what a stranger said to me while we watched, the call I was on when the phones went down, and what the day did to me for years afterward, which I did not have the words for at the time. I get into the politics only at the end, because the politics came at the end.
##### If you were there, or you lost someone, I hope this is worth your half hour. If you weren't, I hope it helps you understand the people who were. Either way, it is free, and it always will be.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuYmx1ZWFtcC5jby9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.OVhGi1ckh53hmZw7cYMnvr2V69suyNkKot25lS_aM4Y?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=215273099)
_**-- Cliff**_
* * *
Cliff has written about September 11 before. He had never sat down and told it straight through, so on the twenty-fifth anniversary he did, from a porch in Cincinnati in a Yankees cap, for the nearly three hundred people who found the stream without an email. He was working a city council primary in lower Manhattan that morning and was on his way to the World Trade Center on a campaign errand when the phone rang.
What follows is not a rant. It is what he saw from the corner of Delancey and Ridge, what a stranger beside him said, the call he was on when every phone in New York went dead, and the years it took before he could hear the date on the radio without going somewhere dark. Near the end he turns to what the day did to the country, and to the Republicans he says used it.
#### Five Things You Will Hear
* The sky that morning, and why he still cannot decide whether he noticed it at the time or only afterward (02:58).
* Delancey and Ridge, the second plane coming in "like slow motion," and the seven words a stranger said next to him (06:50).
* Why he started running toward the towers, why he stopped, and the twenty minutes that separated him from being underneath them (10:25).
* The ten-minute phone call with his father that the network cut off, and why the date now belongs to his dad too (12:53).
* The bus that backfired in Washington three weeks later, and the decision that eventually landed him in Cincinnati (25:23).

name: Congressman Eric Burlison
subject: A quiet moment of prayer for America
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Eric Burlison for Congress
body:
Remembering the innocent lives lost and the brave souls who ran toward danger| | |
---
Twenty-five years ago today, our nation changed forever. On September 11, 2001, an act of unimaginable evil sought to break the spirit of the United States. **Thousands of innocent souls – mothers, fathers, sons, daughters, and friends – were taken from us far too soon at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and in a quiet field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.** Yet, in our darkest hour, the world witnessed the unmatched courage and resolve that defines the American spirit. We saw first responders – firefighters, police officers, and paramedics – unhesitatingly run directly toward danger, risking and giving their lives to save strangers. We saw everyday citizens demonstrate incredible heroism, holding the line in the skies above Pennsylvania to protect countless others. In the days, weeks, and years that followed, a brave generation of young Americans stepped forward to answer the call of duty in our Armed Forces to defend our nation’s freedom. **A quarter-century later, the passage of time has not diminished our sorrow, nor has it weakened our solemn pledge:_We Will Never Forget._** Today, I ask you to join my family in pausing to honor the sacred memory of all those we lost on 9/11. Let us keep the families who still carry the quiet weight of grief in our daily prayers. And let us renew our profound gratitude for the brave law enforcement officers, firefighters, healthcare workers, and military service members who sacrifice so much to keep our communities and country safe. **In the face of heartbreak, America united as one people under God. May we always remember that unity, honor those heroes, and cherish the precious gift of American freedom.** God bless the memory of the fallen, God bless our first responders and military heroes, and God bless the United States of America. In solemn remembrance, _Rep. Eric Burlison_
